newsitem.title: UK: Global LPG strongest in Europe, slipping elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: Global LPG strongest in Europe, slipping elsewhere.

text.p: Prices for propane, the grade of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) used for heating, continued to firm throughout the week in Europe while levels softened in the U.S. and interest withered in East Asia.

In Northwest Europe, the $420 a tonne barrier was breached for large cif cargoes as prices continued their relentles rise. A Scandinavian seller said that, if his company had a cargo available for loading next week, he would be asking at least $430 a tonne now, and others agree this is the current offer price.
"I believe it will get stronger", said a trader. "Demand into Europe is extremely strong and we are already supplying at maximum capacity. You can't get prompt tonnes", he added.

And the demand is purely for prompt material, he continued. "That's the nature of the market - you need tonnes now, not next week or next month." He estimated that storage in Northern Europe has been drawn down by 100,000 tonnes over the winter and tanks are now effectively empty.

As prices in Europe have risen, so in the U.S. they have softened over the week as the market believes it has enough supply to get through even a cold February. This has increased the theoretical opportunity to move product transatlantic, but so far this has not happened.

"We're now $120 above the States. In theory, there should have been an armada", said a dealer. "In practice it hasn't happened as shipping is as tight as product". He added that cargoes from the U.S. take a long time to load, up to nine days, as material has to be refrigerated before being transferred to tankers. This increases the risk that prices may have fallen by February when product could first arrive in Europe.

Product is also moving from the Mediterranean to Northwest Europe to take advantage of higher prices. Algerian state company Sonatrach confirmed that propane is loading now to move north, and the Mediterranean market is tightening in consequence.

One trader suggested that Mediterranean sellers are already asking $400 a tonne cif Lavera in the French Mediterranean, although buyers have yet to approach these levels. There is a high offtake from consumers in Italy, France and elsewhere, and not much prompt availability.
As in northwest Europe, the key is timing, he added. "It's a timing issue more than a product issue. There's plenty of availability in February, but people need it now."
The strength in large cargoes has filtered down to smaller vessels. Seagoing coasters have traded as high as $435 a tonne on Teesside in the North East of England, and are offered higher still.

The strength on coasters was compounded by a minor problem on a pipeline from the North Sea's Ekofisk field, with a four-metre section needing replacement because of corrosion. But a trader was dismissive of this, saying that the market was fundamantally strong and a minor problem like that made no significant difference.

While Europe remained strong, interest has faded significantly in East Asia as prices are still too high for all non-essential buyers. A Japanese trader said that there were several requirements now seen in Japan, although buyers were not willing to move until prices soften.

Assuming the February Saudi Contract Price (CP) falls by $5 or $10 a tonne, as many expect, he believed there would be buying interest from Japan at February CP +$30 a tonne, with sellers asking for $5 a tonne more than this.
And Chinese demand has also failed to pick up, despite the anticipated rush for product to coincide with celebrations for the lunar New Year at the beginning of February.

In the Middle East Gulf, price levels are also falling with little interest seen for lifting spot cargoes. One dealer assessed levels for both propane and butane at between CP +0/5, with the first spot tender for February, the T1 tender, thought to have gone for little above the Saudi CP for January - $330 a tonne.
The second tender, T2, closes on Friday, and an Adgas tender for 31,500 tonnes of propane and 13,500 tonnes of butane closes on 20 January, with bids valid until 22 January, dealers said.
